Containment panels listed to drop away on heat
or sprinklers inside the contained aisle

questions.prompt: Why Fluidstack?

Story 5 plus the research in the playbook

questions.prompt: A time you rejected a standard approach.
beats: Texas BESS · 20 flame detectors · fault appears past ~7 connected
Measured, didn't hunt: 0.5–4 V induced per leg → ~7 modules sum past 0.4 V
Shielded, untwisted: a shield blocks electric fields, twisting cancels magnetic
Client tried cheaper fixes → I proved it with twisted cable laid on the ground
Re-pull ~2 weeks, commissioned → check cable data sheets at submittal
Show the reasoning chain, not the rebellion
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Values and judgment (the 65%)

questions.prompt: The fire pump misses the 150% point at acceptance.
questions.followUp: The test setup checks out and it still misses — what then?
beats: Check the test first: calibrated gauges, pitot readings, nozzle sizes, measured speed with affinity correction
Then suction: a partly closed valve, strainer debris, air entrainment
Then the pump: rotation, impeller debris
Compare to the certified shop curve
Genuine shortfall = manufacturer claim and an impairment plan

questions.prompt: The schedule says skip or compress a test. What do you do?

Life-safety and code-required tests are not negotiable
Tests that can run in parallel get re-sequenced
Anything deferred gets a documented risk acceptance, an impairment entry and a fire watch
"Velocity is knowing which unknowns actually block you" — their words, your method

questions.prompt: Tell me about working with a third-party commissioning agent or an AHJ.

A script they've seen in advance, a pre-test that has already passed, one person running the room

questions.prompt: Walk me through the Cx levels for a pre-action system — what each level proves and what you'd test there.
beats: L1 — factory acceptance / factory witness test: the equipment meets spec before it ships — the releasing panel factory test

L2 — delivery and installation verification: what arrived matches the submittal and is installed per design and listing — hangers and seismic bracing, sprinkler temperature ratings and obstructions around containment
L3 — start-up / pre-functional: each component runs on its own — the dry / pre-action air test, program loaded, 100% point-to-point
L4 — functional performance test: every sequence, including failure and degraded modes, against the Basis of Design — the pre-action trip with water delivery time

L5 — integrated systems test: all systems work together under simulated load and utility failure, the way Ops will live with them — release signals to BMS / EPMS, fire alarm through a utility failure onto generator. End on IST.
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Commissioning technical (the 35%)

followUps.prompt: Say the L3 point-to-point was sampled, not 100%. Do you start L4?
beats: L3 is 100% point-to-point, not a sample
The script's prerequisites: prior level signed off before L4 starts
A deferral is a documented risk acceptance, an impairment entry and a fire watch — not a quiet skip

followUps.prompt: The air test at L3 — numbers, and the section?
beats: Dry and double-interlock air test: 40 psi for 24 h, loss ≤ 1.5 psi
Air supply: restores normal air pressure within 30 min (NFPA 13 §8.2.6.3)

questions.prompt: The 24-hour air test lost 3 psi. What next?
beats: It fails: the limit is 1.5 psi loss over 24 h at 40 psi (NFPA 13 §29.2.2)
Find the leak — grooved couplings and threaded joints are the usual places
Fix it and run the air test again
Check the air supply too: it has to restore normal pressure within 30 min
questions.source: Pre-action

followUps.prompt: Say it fails again on the retest. Now what?
beats: Find the leak again — grooved couplings and threaded joints are the usual places
Fix it and run the full 24 h again; the criterion doesn't move: loss ≤ 1.5 psi at 40 psi
The L4 script's first prerequisite is hydro and air test passed — L4 doesn't start until it does

followUps.prompt: Why not just top the air up and keep going? The compressor can hold it.
beats: The test is 40 psi for 24 h with loss ≤ 1.5 psi — the leak is what you're finding, at grooved couplings and threaded joints
The air supply is its own test: it must restore normal pressure within 30 minutes
Automatic air supervision is required above 20 sprinklers

questions.prompt: The fire pump misses the 150% point at acceptance. Walk me through what you check, in order.
beats: Check the test first: calibrated gauges, pitot readings, nozzle sizes
Measured speed with affinity correction
Then suction: a partly closed valve, strainer debris, air entrainment
Then the pump: rotation, impeller debris
Compare to the certified shop curve
Genuine shortfall = manufacturer claim and an impairment plan
questions.source: Likely questions and day-of checklist › Commissioning technical (the 35%)

followUps.prompt: Say the speed correction alone brings the point onto the curve. Where does that leave you?

Plot net pressure, not discharge pressure
Curve match is within the accuracy of the test equipment — the 95% / 5% figure is NFPA 25's annual test, not acceptance

followUps.prompt: Say suction checks out, the pump checks out, and it's still short. What are you writing up?
beats: Genuine shortfall = manufacturer claim
…and an impairment plan for the building while it's unresolved
Life-safety issues close before turnover; anything else carried into operations needs a documented risk acceptance

followUps.prompt: How did you catch the wrong-COLO release?
beats: Running cause and effect zone by zone against the sequence of operations, watching which valve actually operated, not just that a release output went active
It was double interlock, so that system primed but never filled; the releases for two COLOs were swapped
I verified the release relay for every system and corrected the programming to the sequence of operations

followUps.prompt: What thresholds did you set, and why?
beats: The factory defaults were Fire 1 at 2 %/ft and Fire 2 at 4 %/ft, no more sensitive than a spot photoelectric detector (roughly 0.5–4 %/ft)
We set Fire 1 to 0.0625 %/ft and Fire 2 to 1 %/ft for very early detection
Tie the new settings to the alarm philosophy: Alert and Action call Ops, Fire 1 is the building alarm, Fire 2 releases

Time the transfer and walk every load in the table

followUps.prompt: What does fire alarm have to carry on secondary power, and where's that from?

Or an automatic-starting generator plus dedicated batteries with 4 h of capacity

beats: Barometric relief or relief damper
The fan's VFD setpoint
Sensor location
A stair tighter than designed
Then run the open-door case before retuning
Too high fails door force (30 lbf); too low lets smoke in

followUps.prompt: Why not just turn the fan's VFD down until the number's right?
beats: Run the open-door case before retuning
Too high fails door force; too low lets smoke in

followUps.prompt: What's the door-force limit, and the NFPA 92 minimum across a barrier?
beats: Door opening force ≤ 30 lbf
Pressure difference, sprinklered space (NFPA 92): ≥ 0.05 in. w.c.
At L4 you measure pressure across every barrier and every door force, zone by zone

questions.prompt: What's on your sprinkler acceptance checklist?

Hydros — underground and aboveground
Air test if dry
Inspector's test and tamper timing
Main drain baseline
Backflow forward flow
Signals to central station, then certificates

followUps.prompt: Say it's a wet system. What drops off the list?
beats: Air test if dry — drops off on a wet system
On dry systems, trip test: time to trip and time to water at the test connection — also dry only
Everything else stays: flush → hydros → inspector's test and tamper timing → main drain baseline → backflow forward flow → signals to central station → certificates

followUps.prompt: The backflow forward-flow test — at what flow?
beats: Forward-flow test at system demand, including hose where applicable (NFPA 13 / NFPA 24)
Hose allowance: Light 100 gpm / 30 min · Ordinary 250 gpm / 60–90 min · Extra 500 gpm / 90–120 min (NFPA 13 Table 19.2.3.1.2)

beats: 8 COLOs · 20 VESDAs · no drawings — waiting wasn't an option

Counted holes, paced runs → only 4 pipe variations → 4 designs, not 20 (80% less)
Thresholds, airflow, transport time on every pipe; damaged pipe found and fixed

followUps.prompt: How did you test transport time?
beats: Smoke at the end cap of every pipe, timed against the ASPIRE calc and NFPA 72's 120-second limit
Normalized airflow and measured transport time on every pipe; the high-flow faults turned out to be damaged pipe above the ceiling, which we repaired

followUps.prompt: Why not wait for drawings?
beats: None existed, and the detectors were at defaults, so the risk was in leaving it as it was
Waiting for as-builts that didn't exist wasn't an option — I started with the data: pulled the configuration from all twenty detectors

questions.prompt: Walk me through the Li-ion off-gas scenario at IST — off-gas, BMS trip, exhaust — through the utility drop.
beats: Off-gas alarm — off-gas detection (e.g., Li-ion Tamer) installed per the manufacturer, test-gas response proven; typically 2–30 min of warning before thermal runaway
BMS isolates the affected string — contactors open; E-stop works; status reaches the FACP or BMS
Exhaust starts and proves flow — sized to hold ≤ 25% LFL (or continuous ≥ 1 cfm/ft², supervised); airflow proven; fan failure alarms
Alarm to Ops
If smoke or heat follows: building alarm and sprinklers — 0.3 gpm/ft² over the room or 2,500 ft², whichever is smaller (IFC 1207.5.5)
Drop utility mid-event and confirm detection, BMS and exhaust stay powered
questions.source: Battery and BESS › L5 scenario

followUps.prompt: Why not let the BMS handle it alone? It already trips on temperature.
beats: It's a layered defense proven in order: off-gas detection catches a failing cell, the BMS isolates it, exhaust keeps vent gas below 25% LFL, explosion control handles what exhaust can't, and water controls the fire
Off-gas detection buys 2–30 min of warning before thermal runaway; the BMS trips on off-gas, over-temperature and voltage faults
Vent gas is flammable, so explosion control matters

followUps.prompt: Say the IST matrix row for Li-ion off-gas is blank under building alarm and central station. Do you test those cells?
beats: The matrix row: Li-ion off-gas, UPS room → building alarm —, central station —, BMS trips the string, exhaust on, BMS / EPMS ●
The blank cells get tested too — proving an output does not happen is half the job
Example only — the BOD decides every cell

questions.prompt: An ASD detector is in flow fault every morning. What's your list?
beats: Pressure-zone mismatch between sampling and exhaust is the most common source of flow faults
Return the detector exhaust to the sampled zone when it sits in a different pressure zone (under-floor, duct, plenum)
High-flow faults: damaged pipe — in Story 2 it was above the ceiling
Re-check flow with CRAHs in every mode, including one unit failed
Normalize airflow only after pipes are clean and HVAC runs in its normal mode

The faults themselves have to work: verify each pipe's flow reading, then force low-flow (block the inlet) and high-flow (break the pipe) faults

followUps.prompt: Say the faults only show up when one CRAH is down.
